lungs.name: Lungs
lungs.desc: Handle gas exchange: take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.
lungs.location: Chest cavity on both sides of the heart; they rest on the diaphragm

facts.alveoli: Contain hundreds of millions of alveoli
facts.lobes: The right lung has three lobes, the left has two
facts.breaths: An adult takes 12–20 breaths per minute

daily: The right lung is larger than the left: the heart takes up room on the left
The alveoli add up to 50–75 m², about the floor area of a small flat
At rest, each breath moves about 0.5 L of air
Lungs have no muscles: the diaphragm and the muscles between the ribs stretch them
The left lung has a cardiac notch, a hollow that makes room for the heart

liver.name: Liver
liver.desc: Filters the blood, neutralises harmful substances and produces bile.
liver.location: Upper right abdomen under the diaphragm; the left lobe crosses the midline

facts.largest_gland: The largest gland in the body

daily: Weighs about 1.5 kg, making it the heaviest internal organ
About 1.5 L of blood passes through it every minute
It gets blood from two sources: the hepatic artery and the portal vein
It makes 0.5–1 L of bile a day
It can grow back even after up to two thirds of it is removed

gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
gallbladder.desc: Stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the intestine when you eat.
gallbladder.location: Under the liver on the right, in a hollow on its lower surface; its tip sticks out below the liver's edge

facts.contracts: After a fatty meal it contracts and pushes bile into the duodenum

daily: Bile gets thicker inside it as water is absorbed
Bile breaks fat into tiny droplets, so enzymes can digest it more easily
You can live without it: bile then flows straight into the intestine

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.desc: Churns food with gastric juice and starts digesting proteins.
stomach.location: Upper left abdomen, below the diaphragm and the liver

facts.acid: Its hydrochloric acid is strong, and mucus protects the stomach walls
facts.digestion_time: Food stays in it for 2–4 hours

daily: The surface layer of its lining renews every 3–5 days
An empty stomach holds about 50 mL and can stretch dozens of times larger
Helicobacter pylori, the bacterium behind ulcers, was only discovered in 1982
A rumbling tummy is gas and fluid moving as the stomach walls contract
It produces about 2 L of gastric juice a day

intestines.name: Intestines
intestines.desc: Finish digestion and absorb nutrients and water.
intestines.location: Abdominal cavity: the small intestine in the centre, framed by the large intestine

facts.small_length: The small intestine is about 6 m long
facts.large_length: The large intestine is about 1.5 m
facts.bacteria: Trillions of helpful bacteria live here

daily: Villi and folds expand the absorbing surface to about 30 m²
The gut wall holds about 500 million neurons, which is why it is called the “second brain”
About 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut
The cells of the lining are fully replaced every 3–5 days
One hypothesis says the appendix keeps a reserve of helpful bacteria

kidneys.name: Kidneys
kidneys.desc: Clean waste from the blood and regulate the body's water balance.
kidneys.location: Against the back wall of the abdomen on either side of the spine, at the level of the lower ribs

facts.fist: A pair of organs, each about the size of a fist
facts.blood_flow: About 1.2 L of blood passes through them every minute
facts.urine: They make urine, which flows down the ureters into the bladder

daily: They filter about 180 L of primary urine a day, yet only about 1.5 L leaves the body
Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, tiny filters
The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left: the liver presses on it from above
They make erythropoietin, a hormone that triggers red blood cell production
A person can live a full life with one healthy kidney

heart.name: Heart
heart.desc: A muscular pump that drives blood through the vessels.
heart.location: Chest cavity between the lungs, about two thirds of it left of the midline

facts.fist: Roughly the size of a fist
facts.chambers: Has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles

daily: At rest it pumps about 5 L of blood a minute
Its rhythm comes from a built-in pacemaker, the sinus node
The “lub-dub” sound is the valves snapping shut
Adult heart muscle cells renew very slowly, about 1% a year
In an embryo the heart starts beating around the third to fourth week

brain.name: Brain
brain.desc: Controls the whole body: thinking, memory, movement and the senses.
brain.location: Inside the skull; it joins the spinal cord through the foramen magnum

facts.energy: Uses about 20% of the body's energy

daily: The brain itself feels no pain: its tissue has no pain receptors
About 60% of the brain's dry mass is fat
The brain floats in cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions blows
The left hemisphere controls the right side of the body, and vice versa
During sleep the brain clears out waste products more actively

thyroid.name: Thyroid gland
thyroid.desc: Makes hormones that control metabolism, growth and body heat.
thyroid.location: Front of the neck, below the thyroid cartilage of the larynx

facts.butterfly: Shaped like a butterfly, it sits on the windpipe below the larynx
facts.iodine: It needs iodine from food to work

daily: It is named after the nearby thyroid cartilage, which looks like a shield
Iodised salt was introduced to fight goitre caused by iodine deficiency
The hormones T3 and T4 are named after the number of iodine atoms in each molecule
It makes calcitonin, which lowers calcium levels in the blood
Thyroid disorders are several times more common in women than in men

spleen.name: Spleen
spleen.desc: Filters the blood, removes old red blood cells and supports the immune system.
spleen.location: Upper left abdomen behind the stomach, level with ribs 9–11

facts.reserve: Keeps a reserve of blood and platelets
facts.live_without: You can live without it: the liver and lymph nodes take over part of its work

daily: About 12 cm long, roughly the size of a fist
The white pulp works for immunity, the red pulp filters the blood
Before birth, the spleen makes blood cells
With mononucleosis, contact sports are off limits: an enlarged spleen can rupture
About one in ten people has an accessory spleen, a small lobe next to the main one

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.desc: Releases digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.
pancreas.location: Behind the stomach, across the abdomen: the head by the duodenum, the tail by the spleen

facts.juice: Releases 1–1.5 L of digestive juice a day
facts.islets: The islets of Langerhans keep track of blood sugar
facts.length: About 15–20 cm long, it lies behind the stomach

daily: The name comes from Greek for “all flesh”
The islets of Langerhans make up only 1–2% of its mass
The gland holds 1 to 3 million islets of Langerhans
Insulin was isolated in 1921, and diabetes stopped being a death sentence
Its juice is alkaline: it neutralises the acid coming from the stomach

bladder.name: Urinary bladder
bladder.desc: Stores urine coming from the kidneys and empties it out of the body.
bladder.location: In the pelvis, just behind the pubic symphysis

facts.urge: The urge to urinate starts at about 200–300 mL
facts.stretch: Its muscular wall stretches like a balloon

daily: It is lined with a special epithelium that stretches without tearing
The ureters push urine along in waves several times a minute
People usually urinate 4–8 times a day
The muscle of its wall is called the detrusor, from Latin for “to push out”
A full bladder rises above the pubic bone and can be felt

esophagus.name: Esophagus
esophagus.desc: A muscular tube that carries swallowed food and water from the throat to the stomach.
esophagus.location: In the neck and chest: behind the trachea and heart, in front of the spine; passes through the diaphragm into the abdomen

facts.peristalsis: Food travels down it in 5–10 seconds, pushed by waves of contraction called peristalsis
facts.sphincter: A ring of muscle (sphincter) at the bottom keeps stomach contents from flowing back up

daily: Thanks to peristalsis you can swallow even while standing on your head
Heartburn is acidic stomach content flowing back into the esophagus
Between swallows its walls are pressed together and the passage is nearly closed
The upper part of its wall is skeletal muscle and the lower part is smooth muscle
It has three natural narrowings where swallowed objects most often get stuck

trachea.name: Trachea
trachea.desc: The windpipe: air travels through it from the larynx to the bronchi and lungs.
trachea.location: Front of the neck and upper chest, in front of the esophagus; at the bottom it splits into the two main bronchi

facts.length: About 10–12 cm long in an adult
facts.rings: Its frame is 16–20 C-shaped rings of cartilage, open at the back
facts.cilia: Tiny hairs (cilia) in its lining constantly sweep dust and mucus up toward the throat

daily: Its soft back wall without cartilage lets the esophagus widen when you swallow
The point where it splits into two bronchi is called the bifurcation, or carina
The isthmus of the thyroid gland lies on its front
An opening cut into it (a tracheostomy) lets a person breathe bypassing the larynx
Its cartilage rings keep the tube from collapsing when you breathe in

adrenals.name: Adrenal glands
adrenals.desc: A pair of endocrine glands that make adrenaline, cortisol and aldosterone.
adrenals.location: Behind the abdominal cavity (retroperitoneum), on top of the upper poles of the kidneys

facts.layers: The outer layer (cortex) makes cortisol and aldosterone; the inner layer (medulla) makes adrenaline and noradrenaline
facts.shape: The right one is shaped like a triangle, the left one like a crescent

daily: Adrenaline triggers the fight-or-flight response: the heart speeds up and the pupils widen
Cortisol peaks in the morning, soon after waking up
Aldosterone makes the kidneys hold on to sodium and water, keeping blood pressure up
The word “adrenaline” comes from Latin ad renes, “near the kidneys”
The cortex also releases small amounts of sex hormones

appendix.name: Appendix
appendix.desc: A worm-like pouch of the cecum: a narrow tube closed at one end, with a lot of lymphoid tissue in its wall.
appendix.location: Lower right abdomen (right iliac region), attached to the cecum

facts.size: Usually 7–10 cm long and less than 1 cm thick
facts.position: Its position varies: it may lie behind the cecum or hang down into the pelvis
facts.lymphoid: The lymphoid tissue in its wall helps protect the gut from infection

daily: Acute appendicitis is one of the most common reasons for emergency abdominal surgery
Appendicitis pain often starts near the navel and then moves to the lower right
One hypothesis says it is a reserve of helpful gut bacteria
Its Latin name vermiformis means “worm-shaped”
You can live without it: removing it usually does not affect health

rectum.name: Rectum
rectum.desc: The last part of the large intestine: it stores feces and pushes them out of the body.
rectum.location: In the pelvis, in front of the sacrum and coccyx; behind the bladder in men and behind the uterus in women

facts.ampulla: Its wider lower part is called the ampulla
facts.sphincters: The exit is closed by two rings of muscle, the internal and external sphincters

daily: Despite its name (Latin for “straight”), it curves along the sacrum
The urge to empty the bowels comes when the ampulla stretches
You can control the external sphincter at will, but not the internal one
Stool tests for hidden blood and colonoscopy help find cancer early
Medicines given as suppositories are quickly absorbed through its wall into the blood

uterus.name: Uterus
uterus.desc: A hollow muscular organ of the female reproductive system where a baby grows during pregnancy.
uterus.location: In the pelvis, between the urinary bladder (in front) and the rectum (behind)

facts.size: About 7–8 cm long and about 50 g in a woman who has not given birth
facts.pregnancy: During pregnancy its mass grows to about 1 kg
facts.endometrium: Its inner lining, the endometrium, renews itself in every menstrual cycle

daily: The fallopian tubes connect its cavity with the abdominal cavity near the ovaries
Fertilization usually happens not in the uterus itself but in a fallopian tube
Its narrow lower part is called the cervix and opens into the vagina
The contractions of its muscular wall during childbirth are called labor contractions
The HPV vaccine prevents most cases of cervical cancer

ovaries.name: Ovaries
ovaries.desc: A pair of female sex glands where egg cells mature and the hormones estrogen and progesterone are made.
ovaries.location: In the pelvis, on both sides of the uterus, next to the open ends of the fallopian tubes

facts.size: Each is about 3–4 cm long, roughly the size and shape of an almond
facts.follicles: At birth they hold about 1–2 million immature eggs (follicles)
facts.ovulations: Only about 400–500 eggs mature and are released over a lifetime

daily: The release of a mature egg is called ovulation and usually happens once a month
The egg is one of the largest human cells: about 0.1 mm across
The burst follicle turns into the corpus luteum, which releases progesterone
The supply of follicles shrinks with age, and ovulation stops at menopause
Usually only one egg matures in each cycle

prostate.name: Prostate
prostate.desc: A male gland that makes part of the seminal fluid; it surrounds the beginning of the urethra.
prostate.location: In the pelvis, below the urinary bladder and in front of the rectum

facts.chestnut: About the size and shape of a chestnut
facts.weight: Weighs about 20 g in an adult man
facts.secretion: Its secretion makes up about a third of the seminal fluid

daily: It often grows with age and can make urination harder
A doctor can feel it through the wall of the rectum
A PSA (prostate-specific antigen) blood test helps detect its diseases
Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men
Enzymes in its secretion make the seminal fluid more liquid

aorta.name: Aorta
aorta.desc: The largest artery: it leaves the left ventricle of the heart and carries oxygen-rich blood to the whole body.
aorta.location: Starts at the heart, arches above it and runs down along the spine into the abdomen, where it splits into the two iliac arteries

facts.diameter: About 2.5–3 cm wide in an adult, roughly the width of a thumb
facts.elastic: Its elastic wall stretches with every heartbeat and smooths out the surges of blood
facts.branches: Arteries to the head and arms leave the arch; arteries to the abdominal organs and kidneys leave the abdominal part

daily: At rest about 5 liters of blood pass through it every minute
In an adult it is about 30 cm long, from the heart to the lower abdomen
The pulse in your neck and wrist is a wave that each heartbeat sends along the aorta and its branches
Its wall has three layers; the middle one is made of elastic fibers and muscle cells
The aorta passes into the abdomen through its own opening in the diaphragm

vena_cava.name: Venae cavae
vena_cava.desc: The two largest veins, superior and inferior: they collect oxygen-poor blood from the whole body and bring it to the right atrium.
vena_cava.location: The superior one is in the chest above the heart, to the right of the aorta; the inferior one runs up from the pelvis to the right of the spine, behind the liver, to the heart

facts.widest: The inferior one is the widest vein in the body, about 2–3 cm across
facts.pressure: Blood pressure inside them is very low: muscle contractions and breathing help push the blood toward the heart
facts.no_valves: Unlike the veins of the legs, they have no valves inside

daily: The inferior one drains the legs, pelvis, kidneys and liver; the superior one drains the head, neck and arms
The superior one is short, only about 7 cm long
When you breathe in, pressure in the chest drops and blood flows back to the heart faster
The Latin word cavus means 'hollow': these veins have a very wide channel
The inferior one passes through its own opening in the central tendon of the diaphragm

spinal_cord.name: Spinal cord and nerves
spinal_cord.desc: A cord of nerve tissue inside the spine: it carries signals between the brain and the body and handles simple reflexes. 31 pairs of spinal nerves branch off it.
spinal_cord.location: Inside the vertebral canal, from the base of the skull to the first or second lumbar vertebra; branches spread out to the arms, legs and body wall

facts.length: About 45 cm long and roughly as thick as a little finger
facts.reflex: The knee-jerk reflex is handled here, without the brain
facts.pairs: 31 pairs of nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal

daily: The longest nerve in the body is the sciatic nerve: it runs from the lower back to the foot
Signals travel along thick nerve fibers at up to 100 m/s
Below the second lumbar vertebra the canal holds only a 'horse's tail' of nerve roots, so lumbar punctures are done lower down
The 'funny bone' is really the ulnar nerve, which lies right under the skin at the elbow
Like the brain, it is bathed in cerebrospinal fluid

thymus.name: Thymus
thymus.desc: An immune-system gland where T cells, the white blood cells that recognize invaders, mature and are 'trained'.
thymus.location: In the chest behind the breastbone, above the heart and in front of the large blood vessels

facts.childhood: It works hardest in childhood; by old age it is almost entirely replaced by fat
facts.weight: Weighs about 30–40 g in a teenager
facts.lobes: Its two lobes look like the prongs of a fork, which gave it its Russian name

daily: The T in 'T cells' stands for thymus
In a newborn it weighs about 10–15 g, larger for the body's size than at any later age
Here white blood cells learn not to attack the body's own cells
Its hormones, thymosins, help immune cells mature
A baby born without it is almost defenseless against infections

pituitary.name: Pituitary gland
pituitary.desc: A small gland beneath the brain that conducts the hormone orchestra: it controls the thyroid, adrenal glands, sex glands and growth.
pituitary.location: In a hollow at the base of the skull called the sella turcica, hanging on a stalk below the hypothalamus

facts.size: About the size of a pea; weighs about 0.5 g
facts.lobes: The front lobe makes hormones; the back lobe stores and releases hormones from the hypothalamus
facts.growth: Its growth hormone largely decides how tall a child will grow

daily: Oxytocin and vasopressin enter the blood from its back lobe
It takes orders from the hypothalamus, the part of the brain just above it
Too much growth hormone in an adult causes acromegaly: the hands, feet and facial features grow larger
Its other name, hypophysis, is Greek for 'outgrowth below'
Its hormone prolactin starts the production of breast milk

diaphragm.name: Diaphragm
diaphragm.desc: A dome-shaped muscle that separates the chest cavity from the abdomen and does most of the work of breathing in.
diaphragm.location: Below the lungs and heart, above the liver, stomach and spleen; attached to the lower ribs, breastbone and spine

facts.inhale: When you breathe in it contracts and moves down, and the lungs fill with air
facts.openings: The esophagus, aorta and inferior vena cava pass through it
facts.excursion: In quiet breathing the dome drops 1–2 cm; in deep breathing up to 10 cm

daily: Hiccups are sudden involuntary contractions of this muscle
It works nonstop for life: about 20,000 breaths a day
You can control it on purpose, and in sleep it works on its own
It is driven by the phrenic nerve, which starts up in the neck
Laughing, coughing and sneezing are its work too

lymph_nodes.name: Lymph nodes
lymph_nodes.desc: Pea- or bean-sized filters of lymph: they trap germs and cancer cells, and immune cells learn to fight them there.
lymph_nodes.location: In clusters along the vessels of the body's drainage system: in the neck, armpits and groin, and also in the chest and abdomen

facts.count: There are about 500–700 of them in the body
facts.cold: During a cold the nodes in the neck swell and hurt: an infection is being fought
facts.flow: Lymph flows through them slowly, without a pump: muscle contractions push it along

daily: About 2–3 liters of lymph return to the blood every day
The lymphatic system has no 'heart' of its own
B cells make antibodies, and T cells destroy infected cells
The largest lymphatic vessel, the thoracic duct, empties into the veins at the base of the neck
Doctors feel the nodes in the neck, armpits and groin: their size says a lot about health

food.title: The path of food
food.intro: Let's follow a bite of food from the esophagus to the rectum. The digestive tract is a tube several meters long, helped by the liver, gallbladder and pancreas.

steps.esophagus: A swallowed bite enters the esophagus, a muscular tube behind the trachea. Waves of contraction (peristalsis) push it down in 5–10 seconds — even if you stand on your head.
steps.stomach: The stomach is a bag where food is mixed with acidic gastric juice. Hydrochloric acid kills germs, and the enzyme pepsin starts breaking down proteins. After 2–4 hours the mush moves on in portions into the duodenum.
steps.liver: The liver never touches food, but it makes bile, without which fats are poorly digested. All the blood from the intestines passes through the liver first: harmful substances are neutralized here and glycogen is stored.
steps.gallbladder: Bile from the liver is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder. When fatty food reaches the intestine, the gallbladder contracts and squeezes bile into the duodenum.
steps.pancreas: The pancreas releases juice with enzymes into the same duodenum; they break down proteins, fats and carbohydrates. The juice is alkaline and neutralizes stomach acid.
steps.intestines: In the small intestine digestion is completed, and nutrients are absorbed into the blood through millions of villi. The large intestine absorbs water, and bacteria feed on what we cannot digest ourselves.
steps.appendix: The appendix is a small pouch of the cecum, where the large intestine begins. Its wall is rich in lymphoid tissue, so it is considered part of the gut's immune defense.
steps.rectum: The last stretch is the rectum. Whatever was not used collects here, and two muscle rings — the sphincters — hold it in until you go to the toilet.

air.title: Air and blood
air.intro: How does oxygen get from the air into every cell? Let's follow a breath, then see who carries oxygen around the body and looks after the blood.

steps.trachea: Inhaled air passes through the nose and larynx into the trachea. Rings of cartilage keep it from collapsing, and tiny cilia sweep dust back up to the throat.
steps.lungs: The trachea splits into bronchi, which branch smaller and smaller and end in alveoli — tiny air sacs. Oxygen passes through their thin walls into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes back into the air.
steps.heart: Oxygen-rich blood from the lungs flows into the left side of the heart, which pumps it into the aorta and on to every organ. Meanwhile the right side sends “used” blood back to the lungs.
steps.spleen: The spleen filters the blood, removing old red blood cells and germs, and its lymphoid tissue supports immunity. You can live without it, but defense against some infections is weaker.
steps.diaphragm: Breathing in is mostly the diaphragm's job: the dome of this muscle contracts and moves down, the chest cavity grows, and air flows into the lungs. When it relaxes, you breathe out.

water.title: Cleaning and urine
water.intro: The blood is constantly cleaned of waste, extra water and salts. Let's see how urine is made from it and where it goes.

steps.kidneys: The kidneys filter the blood: more than a thousand liters pass through them each day, yielding about one and a half liters of urine. They also control water, salts and blood pressure.
steps.bladder: Urine flows down the ureters into the bladder. Its wall stretches, and at about 200–300 ml the brain gets the signal: time to go.
steps.prostate: In men the prostate lies just below the bladder, and the start of the urethra runs through it. That is why urinating gets harder when the prostate enlarges with age.

control.title: Control: nerves and hormones
control.intro: The body is controlled in two ways: fast, by nerve signals, and more slowly, by hormones that glands release into the blood.

steps.brain: The brain is the main control center: its signals travel along nerves in fractions of a second. Its hypothalamus commands many glands through the pituitary.
steps.thyroid: The thyroid releases hormones that contain iodine. They set the pace of metabolism: too little makes a person cold and tired, too much makes them lose weight and feel anxious.
steps.adrenals: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. When you are frightened they release adrenaline: the heart beats faster and muscles get ready to act. Cortisol helps cope with stress, and aldosterone keeps salts in balance.
steps.pancreas: The pancreas is also a hormone gland: insulin lowers blood sugar after a meal, and glucagon raises it when we are hungry.
steps.ovaries: The ovaries make the female sex hormones, estrogens and progesterone, which control the menstrual cycle.
steps.spinal_cord: The spinal cord is the main cable: signals travel along it and its 31 pairs of nerves from the brain to the muscles and back. It handles the simplest reflexes by itself.
steps.pituitary: The pituitary is a pea-sized gland under the brain that conducts the other glands: on orders from the hypothalamus it releases hormones that switch on the thyroid, adrenal glands, sex glands and growth.

blood.title: Circles of circulation
blood.intro: Blood keeps going round: from the body to the heart, from the heart to the lungs and back, and then around the whole body again. Let's follow the route.

steps.vena_cava: Blood that has given its oxygen to the body's cells gathers in the two largest veins, the superior and inferior venae cavae, and returns to the heart.
steps.heart: The right side of the heart sends dark venous blood to the lungs: the pulmonary circulation. The left side takes it back, now full of oxygen, and pumps it into the systemic circulation.
steps.lungs: In the alveoli of the lungs the blood gives up carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen, turning bright red.
steps.aorta: From the left ventricle the blood enters the aorta, the main artery of the systemic circulation. Its branches deliver oxygen to the head, arms, abdominal organs and legs.
steps.kidneys: The kidneys receive almost a quarter of all the blood the heart pumps out and clean it of waste. Then the blood flows on into the inferior vena cava, and the circle is closed.

defense.title: Defenders of the body
defense.intro: The immune system is not one organ but a whole network: in some organs defender cells are born and trained, in others they meet the enemy.

steps.thymus: The thymus is a 'school' for T cells: here they learn to tell the body's own cells from foreign ones. It works hardest in childhood.
steps.lymph_nodes: Lymph nodes are filters along the path of lymph. When germs arrive, immune cells multiply and the node swells.
steps.spleen: The spleen filters the blood itself: it removes old red blood cells and bacteria and keeps a reserve of immune cells.
steps.appendix: The wall of the appendix is full of lymphoid tissue: it helps guard the gut and may keep a reserve of helpful bacteria.

diseases._comment: Articles of the disease guide (the Diseases button). Which organ has which disease is in diseases.py.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.desc: An infection of the lung tissue: the alveoli fill with fluid and pus and pass less oxygen into the blood.
pneumonia.symptoms: Cough with phlegm, high fever, shortness of breath, chest pain when breathing, weakness.
pneumonia.causes: Usually bacteria (pneumococcus), less often viruses or fungi. The risk is higher in older people, smokers, after flu and with COPD.
pneumonia.treatment: Bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics, severe cases in hospital with oxygen. Vaccines protect against pneumococcus and flu.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.desc: Long-term inflammation of the airways: in response to triggers they narrow, swell and fill with mucus.
asthma.symptoms: Attacks of breathlessness, wheezing, coughing (often at night), a tight feeling in the chest.
asthma.causes: An inherited tendency and allergies. Attacks are triggered by dust, pollen, pet hair, cold air, exercise and smoke.
asthma.treatment: Inhalers: steroid ones every day to calm the inflammation and reliever ones to open the airways during an attack. Avoiding triggers matters.

copd.name: COPD
copd.desc: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: the airways slowly and permanently narrow and the alveoli break down (emphysema).
copd.symptoms: Breathlessness that grows over years, a long-lasting cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections.
copd.causes: Mostly smoking; less often years of breathing smoke, dust and fumes at work or at home.
copd.treatment: Quitting smoking slows it down. Inhalers open the airways; breathing exercises and flu and pneumococcal vaccines help.

lung_cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the cells of the bronchi or lung tissue; one of the deadliest cancers worldwide.
lung_cancer.symptoms: Few signs for a long time. Later: a persistent cough, blood in phlegm, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss.
lung_cancer.causes: About 85% of cases are linked to smoking. Second-hand smoke, radon, asbestos and air pollution add to the risk.
lung_cancer.treatment: Surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted drugs and immunotherapy, depending on the type and stage.

hepatitis.name: Viral hepatitis
hepatitis.desc: Inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis viruses A, B, C, D or E. B and C can become chronic.
hepatitis.symptoms: Tiredness, nausea, dark urine, jaundice. Chronic hepatitis often goes unnoticed for years.
hepatitis.causes: A and E spread through dirty water and food; B, C and D through blood, shared needles and sex.
hepatitis.treatment: Hepatitis C is cured with antiviral pills, B is kept under control with them. There are vaccines against hepatitis A and B.

fatty_liver.name: Fatty liver disease
fatty_liver.desc: Fat builds up in the liver cells. Over time inflammation can follow, and then cirrhosis.
fatty_liver.symptoms: Usually none; sometimes heaviness under the right ribs and tiredness. It is often found by chance on an ultrasound.
fatty_liver.causes: Excess weight, type 2 diabetes, lack of exercise, and alcohol.
fatty_liver.treatment: Losing 7–10% of body weight, exercise, avoiding alcohol and treating diabetes. In the early stages the liver recovers.

cirrhosis.name: Cirrhosis
cirrhosis.desc: The end stage of many liver diseases: the tissue is replaced by scars and the liver can no longer do its job.
cirrhosis.symptoms: Weakness, jaundice, swelling and fluid in the abdomen, bleeding from swollen veins in the esophagus, confusion.
cirrhosis.causes: Most often years of heavy drinking, chronic hepatitis B and C, and fatty liver disease.
cirrhosis.treatment: Stopping the cause (virus, alcohol) and treating complications. A liver transplant saves lives in severe cases.

liver_cancer.name: Liver cancer
liver_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the liver cells (hepatocellular carcinoma). It usually develops in a liver with cirrhosis.
liver_cancer.symptoms: Heaviness and pain under the right ribs, weight loss, jaundice; almost no signs early on.
liver_cancer.causes: Cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B and C, alcohol, fatty liver disease.
liver_cancer.treatment: Removing part of the liver, a transplant, destroying the tumour from inside, medicines. People with cirrhosis are checked regularly to catch it early.

gallstones.name: Gallstones
gallstones.desc: Stones form in the gallbladder from parts of bile, most often cholesterol.
gallstones.symptoms: Often none. If a stone blocks the duct: biliary colic, severe pain under the right ribs after a fatty meal.
gallstones.causes: Too much cholesterol in bile, excess weight, rapid weight loss, pregnancy; more common in women over 40.
gallstones.treatment: Stones that cause no trouble are usually left alone. With attacks of colic the gallbladder is removed, usually through small cuts.

cholecystitis.name: Cholecystitis
cholecystitis.desc: Inflammation of the gallbladder, usually because a stone has blocked its outlet.
cholecystitis.symptoms: Severe constant pain under the right ribs, fever, nausea and vomiting.
cholecystitis.causes: Gallstones in 9 cases out of 10: bile gets trapped and becomes infected.
cholecystitis.treatment: Fasting, pain relief and antibiotics in hospital, then removal of the gallbladder.

gastritis.name: Gastritis
gastritis.desc: Inflammation of the stomach lining, sudden or long-lasting.
gastritis.symptoms: Pain and burning in the upper abdomen, heaviness after meals, nausea; chronic gastritis often causes no symptoms.
gastritis.causes: The bacterium Helicobacter pylori, painkillers such as ibuprofen and aspirin, alcohol, and less often autoimmune causes.
gastritis.treatment: Antibiotics to clear Helicobacter, acid-reducing medicines, avoiding alcohol and the pills that harm the stomach.

peptic_ulcer.name: Peptic ulcer
peptic_ulcer.desc: A deep sore in the lining of the stomach or duodenum.
peptic_ulcer.symptoms: Upper abdominal pain on an empty stomach or after eating, heartburn. Dangerous complications are bleeding and perforation.
peptic_ulcer.causes: Mostly Helicobacter pylori and anti-inflammatory painkillers; smoking slows healing.
peptic_ulcer.treatment: Antibiotics against Helicobacter and acid-suppressing drugs; the ulcer usually heals within a few weeks.

gerd.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)
gerd.desc: Acidic stomach contents regularly flow back into the esophagus and irritate its wall.
gerd.symptoms: Heartburn, sour burps, pain behind the breastbone, sometimes cough and hoarseness, especially lying down and after meals.
gerd.causes: A weak lower esophageal sphincter, excess weight, overeating, a hiatal hernia, smoking.
gerd.treatment: No food before bed, a raised head of the bed, weight loss, and acid-reducing medicines. Untreated, it can lead to esophagitis and Barrett's esophagus.

stomach_cancer.name: Stomach cancer
stomach_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the cells of the stomach lining.
stomach_cancer.symptoms: At first, vague discomfort in the abdomen and feeling full quickly. Later, weight loss, anaemia, vomiting, black stools.
stomach_cancer.causes: Long-term Helicobacter pylori infection, smoking, a lot of salty and smoked food, family history.
stomach_cancer.treatment: Surgery to remove part or all of the stomach, chemotherapy. Early tumours can sometimes be removed through a gastroscope.

ibs.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
ibs.desc: A problem with how the bowel works, with no visible damage: the gut becomes oversensitive.
ibs.symptoms: Abdominal pain and bloating that ease after a bowel movement; diarrhoea, constipation or both in turn.
ibs.causes: Disturbed signalling between the gut and the nervous system, stress, a past gut infection.
ibs.treatment: Adjusting the diet (for example fewer fermentable carbohydrates), medicines for cramps, diarrhoea or constipation, managing stress.

ibd.name: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis
ibd.desc: Inflammatory bowel diseases: the immune system attacks the wall of the gut. Ulcerative colitis affects the large intestine, Crohn's disease any part of the gut.
ibd.symptoms: Diarrhoea, often with blood, abdominal pain, weight loss, fever; flare-ups alternate with calm periods.
ibd.causes: A mix of genes, a faulty immune response and gut bacteria; smoking makes Crohn's disease worse.
ibd.treatment: Anti-inflammatory and immune-suppressing drugs, biologic medicines, sometimes surgery.

appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.desc: Sudden inflammation of the appendix, the worm-like pouch of the cecum.
appendicitis.symptoms: Pain starts around the navel and moves to the lower right within a few hours; nausea, fever.
appendicitis.causes: The opening of the appendix gets blocked (by a lump of stool or swollen lymphoid tissue) and bacteria multiply inside.
appendicitis.treatment: Urgent surgery to remove the appendix. Without it the appendix can burst and cause peritonitis.

colorectal_cancer.name: Colorectal cancer
colorectal_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the large intestine or rectum; it usually grows over years from a harmless polyp.
colorectal_cancer.symptoms: Blood in the stool, a change in bowel habits, abdominal pain, tiredness from anaemia, weight loss.
colorectal_cancer.causes: Age over 50, family history, a lot of red and processed meat, little fibre, smoking, excess weight.
colorectal_cancer.treatment: Surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. A colonoscopy finds polyps and removes them before they turn into cancer.

kidney_stones.name: Kidney stones
kidney_stones.desc: Stones form in the kidneys from salts in the urine and can slip into the ureter.
kidney_stones.symptoms: Renal colic: sudden, extreme pain in the lower back spreading to the groin, blood in the urine, nausea.
kidney_stones.causes: Too little water, a lot of salt and animal protein, metabolic disorders, family history.
kidney_stones.treatment: Small stones pass on their own with plenty of fluids and pain relief; large ones are broken up with shock waves or removed with a scope.

pyelonephritis.name: Pyelonephritis
pyelonephritis.desc: A bacterial infection of the kidney and its pelvis.
pyelonephritis.symptoms: High fever with chills, pain in the lower back on one side, frequent painful urination.
pyelonephritis.causes: Usually bacteria travel up the ureter from the bladder; the risk is higher with stones, in pregnancy and in women.
pyelonephritis.treatment: Antibiotics; severe cases are treated in hospital.

glomerulonephritis.name: Glomerulonephritis
glomerulonephritis.desc: Inflammation of the glomeruli, the tiny filters of the kidney, usually caused by a mistake of the immune system.
glomerulonephritis.symptoms: Dark, cola-coloured urine, puffy face in the morning, high blood pressure, protein in the urine.
glomerulonephritis.causes: An immune reaction after a strep throat or another infection, autoimmune diseases.
glomerulonephritis.treatment: Drugs that calm the immune inflammation, blood pressure control, less salt.

ckd.name: Chronic kidney disease
ckd.desc: Over years the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter the blood.
ckd.symptoms: Unnoticed for a long time. Later: swelling, weakness, nausea, itching, high blood pressure, anaemia.
ckd.causes: Most often diabetes and high blood pressure, less often glomerulonephritis and inherited diseases.
ckd.treatment: Controlling blood sugar and blood pressure slows it down. In the final stage, dialysis or a kidney transplant is needed.

ihd.name: Coronary heart disease
ihd.desc: The heart muscle does not get enough blood because the coronary arteries are narrowed by fatty plaques.
ihd.symptoms: Pressing chest pain during exertion (angina). If a plaque ruptures and blocks the vessel, it is a heart attack.
ihd.causes: Atherosclerosis caused by high cholesterol, smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes and lack of exercise.
ihd.treatment: Medicines (against clotting, to lower cholesterol), a stent or bypass surgery. Quitting smoking and staying active.

hypertension.name: High blood pressure
hypertension.desc: Blood pressure that stays at 140/90 mmHg or higher.
hypertension.symptoms: Often none, which is why it is called a "silent killer"; sometimes headaches or ringing in the ears.
hypertension.causes: Family history, too much salt, excess weight, alcohol, lack of exercise, stress, age.
hypertension.treatment: Less salt, exercise, weight loss and medicines. Untreated, it raises the risk of stroke, heart attack, heart failure and chronic kidney disease.

arrhythmia.name: Arrhythmias
arrhythmia.desc: Heart rhythm disorders: the heart beats too fast, too slowly or irregularly.
arrhythmia.symptoms: Skipped beats and fluttering in the chest, palpitations, dizziness, fainting.
arrhythmia.causes: Heart disease, thyroid hormones, caffeine, alcohol, imbalanced salts in the blood. The most common one is atrial fibrillation.
arrhythmia.treatment: Medicines, destroying the faulty spot through a catheter, a pacemaker. With atrial fibrillation, blood thinners help prevent a stroke.

heart_failure.name: Heart failure
heart_failure.desc: The heart cannot pump as much blood as the body needs.
heart_failure.symptoms: Breathlessness on exertion and lying flat, swollen legs, getting tired quickly.
heart_failure.causes: A past heart attack, coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, valve disease.
heart_failure.treatment: Medicines that ease the heart's workload and remove extra fluid, less salt, sometimes special pacemakers.

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.desc: A sudden loss of blood flow in the brain: a vessel is blocked by a clot or bursts.
stroke.symptoms: A suddenly drooping face, weakness of an arm or leg on one side, slurred speech. Call an ambulance at once.
stroke.causes: High blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, atherosclerosis, smoking, diabetes.
stroke.treatment: In the first hours the clot is dissolved with a drug or removed through a catheter. Then come rehabilitation and preventing another stroke.

migraine.name: Migraine
migraine.desc: Attacks of strong throbbing headache, often on one side of the head.
migraine.symptoms: Pain for 4–72 hours, nausea, sensitivity to light and sound; some people get an aura (flashes, zigzags) beforehand.
migraine.causes: An inherited feature of the brain. Attacks are triggered by lack of sleep, stress, hunger, alcohol and hormone changes.
migraine.treatment: Painkillers and special drugs (triptans) at the start of an attack; preventive medicines for frequent attacks.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.desc: A tendency to repeated seizures caused by sudden bursts of activity in the brain's nerve cells.
epilepsy.symptoms: Convulsions with loss of consciousness, brief blank spells, strange sensations or movements.
epilepsy.causes: Brain injuries and tumours, stroke, conditions present from birth, genes; often no cause is found.
epilepsy.treatment: Anti-seizure medicines work for most people; sometimes surgery.

alzheimer.name: Alzheimer's disease
alzheimer.desc: A slow loss of nerve cells in the brain; the most common cause of dementia.
alzheimer.symptoms: First recent events are forgotten, then speech, orientation and the ability to look after oneself decline.
alzheimer.causes: Proteins (beta-amyloid and tau) building up in the brain, age, genes.
alzheimer.treatment: There is no cure. Medicines slightly slow the symptoms; care, activity and support from family matter.

hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
hypothyroidism.desc: The thyroid gland makes too little hormone and metabolism slows down.
hypothyroidism.symptoms: Tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, dry skin, constipation, low mood.
hypothyroidism.causes: Most often Hashimoto's thyroiditis, also removal of the gland and lack of iodine.
hypothyroidism.treatment: A daily thyroxine tablet that replaces the missing hormone.

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease)
hyperthyroidism.desc: The thyroid gland makes too much hormone and metabolism speeds up. A common cause is Graves' disease.
hyperthyroidism.symptoms: Fast heartbeat, weight loss despite a good appetite, sweating, trembling, irritability, sometimes bulging eyes.
hyperthyroidism.causes: In Graves' disease antibodies make the gland work non-stop; less often hormone-producing nodules.
hyperthyroidism.treatment: Medicines that slow the gland, radioactive iodine or surgery.

thyroiditis.name: Hashimoto's thyroiditis
thyroiditis.desc: The immune system attacks the thyroid gland.
thyroiditis.symptoms: Unnoticed for a long time; gradually the signs of hypothyroidism appear, and sometimes the gland gets bigger.
thyroiditis.causes: An inherited tendency; it is much more common in women.
thyroiditis.treatment: The inflammation itself is not treated; when hormone levels fall, thyroxine is taken.

goiter.name: Thyroid nodules
goiter.desc: Lumps form in the thyroid gland; the vast majority are benign.
goiter.symptoms: Usually none; a large nodule can be seen on the neck and may make swallowing harder.
goiter.causes: Lack of iodine, age, family history.
goiter.treatment: Ultrasound check-ups; a suspicious nodule is tested with a needle. Large or dangerous ones are removed.

splenomegaly.name: Enlarged spleen (splenomegaly)
splenomegaly.desc: The spleen grows larger than normal; it is a sign of another illness rather than a disease of its own.
splenomegaly.symptoms: Heaviness under the left ribs, feeling full quickly; often found only during an examination.
splenomegaly.causes: Infections (mononucleosis, malaria), cirrhosis of the liver, blood disorders, lymphomas.
splenomegaly.treatment: The cause is treated. An enlarged spleen ruptures easily, so blows to the abdomen should be avoided.

spleen_rupture.name: Ruptured spleen after an abdominal injury
spleen_rupture.desc: The spleen is full of blood vessels, and a blow can tear it and cause heavy internal bleeding.
spleen_rupture.symptoms: Pain under the left ribs spreading to the left shoulder, pale skin, weakness, falling blood pressure.
spleen_rupture.causes: A blow to the abdomen or left side: a crash, a fall, sport. An enlarged spleen tears more easily.
spleen_rupture.treatment: Small tears sometimes heal under observation; with heavy bleeding the spleen is removed.

spleen_infarction.name: Splenic infarction
spleen_infarction.desc: Part of the spleen dies because the artery feeding it is blocked.
spleen_infarction.symptoms: Sudden pain under the left ribs, sometimes fever; it can also cause no symptoms.
spleen_infarction.causes: Clots in heart and blood disorders, sickle cell disease, a greatly enlarged spleen.
spleen_infarction.treatment: Pain relief and treating the cause; surgery is rarely needed.

hypersplenism.name: Hypersplenism
hypersplenism.desc: An enlarged spleen traps and destroys too many blood cells.
hypersplenism.symptoms: Signs of low blood counts: weakness (anaemia), easy bruising and bleeding, frequent infections.
hypersplenism.causes: Any cause of splenomegaly, most often cirrhosis of the liver with blood backing up.
hypersplenism.treatment: Treating the underlying disease; sometimes the spleen or part of it is removed.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.desc: Inflammation of the pancreas: its enzymes start digesting the gland itself.
pancreatitis.symptoms: Acute: severe upper abdominal pain spreading to the back, vomiting. Chronic: pain after meals, fatty stools, weight loss.
pancreatitis.causes: Mostly alcohol and gallstones blocking the duct outlet.
pancreatitis.treatment: Acute pancreatitis is treated in hospital with fasting, drips and pain relief. Chronic: no alcohol, enzyme tablets.

diabetes.name: Diabetes
diabetes.desc: Blood sugar stays high: there is not enough insulin (type 1) or the cells respond poorly to it (type 2).
diabetes.symptoms: Thirst, frequent urination, weakness, weight loss (in type 1); type 2 can go unnoticed for a long time.
diabetes.causes: Type 1: the immune system destroys the cells of the islets of Langerhans. Type 2: excess weight, lack of exercise, family history.
diabetes.treatment: Type 1: insulin injections. Type 2: diet, exercise, tablets, sometimes insulin. Uncontrolled, it damages the kidneys, eyes, nerves and heart vessels.

pancreatic_cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the pancreas, usually from the cells of its ducts.
pancreatic_cancer.symptoms: Usually found late: jaundice, pain in the upper abdomen and back, weight loss, newly appearing diabetes.
pancreatic_cancer.causes: Smoking, age, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, family history.
pancreatic_cancer.treatment: Surgery if the tumour can be removed, otherwise chemotherapy and relief of symptoms.

cystic_fibrosis.name: Cystic fibrosis
cystic_fibrosis.desc: An inherited disease in which the mucus in many organs becomes thick and sticky.
cystic_fibrosis.symptoms: Blocked ducts of the pancreas cause poor digestion and fatty stools; in the lungs, a persistent cough and infections.
cystic_fibrosis.causes: A faulty CFTR gene inherited from both parents.
cystic_fibrosis.treatment: Enzyme tablets, airway clearance, antibiotics; newer drugs correct how the CFTR protein works.

cystitis.name: Cystitis
cystitis.desc: Inflammation of the urinary bladder, usually from a bacterial infection.
cystitis.symptoms: Frequent painful urges, burning when passing urine, lower abdominal pain, cloudy urine.
cystitis.causes: Bacteria from the gut get into the urethra; women have a shorter urethra, so they get cystitis more often.
cystitis.treatment: Antibiotics and plenty of fluids. Untreated, the infection can spread up to the kidneys (pyelonephritis).

overactive_bladder.name: Overactive bladder
overactive_bladder.desc: The muscle of the bladder wall contracts before the bladder is full.
overactive_bladder.symptoms: Sudden strong urges, frequent urination day and night, sometimes leaking.
overactive_bladder.causes: Often no clear cause; it can come with nervous system diseases and with age.
overactive_bladder.treatment: Bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, medicines that relax the bladder wall.

bladder_stones.name: Bladder stones
bladder_stones.desc: Stones form in the bladder itself when urine stays in it too long.
bladder_stones.symptoms: Lower abdominal pain, a stop-start stream, blood in the urine, frequent urges.
bladder_stones.causes: Incomplete emptying of the bladder, in men most often due to an enlarged prostate; stones coming down from the kidneys.
bladder_stones.treatment: Breaking up and removing them with a scope, and treating the cause of urine retention.

incontinence.name: Urinary incontinence
incontinence.symptoms: Leaking when coughing, laughing or exercising (stress incontinence), or with a sudden strong urge (urge incontinence).
incontinence.causes: Weak pelvic floor muscles after childbirth and with age, overactive bladder, prostate and nervous system diseases.
incontinence.treatment: Pelvic floor exercises, medicines, surgery; it can be treated, and there is no need to feel embarrassed seeing a doctor.

esophagitis.name: Esophagitis
esophagitis.desc: Inflammation of the lining of the esophagus.
esophagitis.symptoms: Heartburn, pain behind the breastbone, pain and difficulty when swallowing.
esophagitis.causes: Most often GERD; also infections, allergy (eosinophilic esophagitis), tablets that get stuck in the esophagus.
esophagitis.treatment: Treating the cause: lowering stomach acid, antifungal drugs, a special diet for allergy.

barrett.name: Barrett's esophagus
barrett.desc: Under the effect of acid, the lining of the lower esophagus changes and comes to look like the lining of the intestine.
barrett.symptoms: No signs of its own, only long-lasting heartburn from GERD.
barrett.causes: Years of stomach contents flowing back; more common in men over 50 with excess weight.
barrett.treatment: Controlling GERD and regular gastroscopy: the changes raise the risk of esophageal cancer and can be removed through a scope.

hiatal_hernia.name: Hiatal hernia
hiatal_hernia.desc: Part of the stomach slides through the opening in the diaphragm from the abdomen into the chest.
hiatal_hernia.symptoms: Often none; otherwise heartburn, burping, pain behind the breastbone, especially lying down.
hiatal_hernia.causes: Tissues weakening with age, raised pressure in the abdomen: excess weight, pregnancy, straining.
hiatal_hernia.treatment: Treating reflux; large hernias are repaired with surgery.

tracheitis.name: Tracheitis
tracheitis.desc: Inflammation of the lining of the trachea, usually together with laryngitis or bronchitis.
tracheitis.symptoms: A dry, tiring cough, a raw feeling behind the breastbone, fever.
tracheitis.causes: Most often cold and flu viruses, less often bacteria; irritation from smoke and cold air.
tracheitis.treatment: It usually clears up on its own: warm drinks, humid air; antibiotics for a bacterial infection.

tracheal_stenosis.name: Tracheal stenosis
tracheal_stenosis.desc: The trachea narrows because of a scar or a tumour, and air passes through it with difficulty.
tracheal_stenosis.symptoms: Breathlessness and noisy, whistling breathing (stridor) that slowly get worse.
tracheal_stenosis.causes: Most often scarring after a long time on a ventilator or after a tracheostomy, less often tumours.
tracheal_stenosis.treatment: Widening the narrow part through a bronchoscope, a stent, or removing that section of the trachea.

foreign_body.name: Inhaled foreign body
foreign_body.desc: An object or piece of food gets into the larynx, trachea or bronchi.
foreign_body.symptoms: Sudden coughing, choking, being unable to speak; if the object moves into a bronchus, a long-lasting cough and pneumonia.
foreign_body.causes: More common in small children (nuts, small toys) and older people; talking and laughing while eating.
foreign_body.treatment: For choking, the Heimlich manoeuvre (thrusts into the upper abdomen). A stuck object is removed with a bronchoscope.

tracheomalacia.name: Tracheomalacia
tracheomalacia.desc: The cartilage of the trachea is too soft, so the tube collapses when breathing out or coughing.
tracheomalacia.symptoms: Noisy breathing, a barking cough, frequent chest infections; in babies from the first weeks of life.
tracheomalacia.causes: Immature cartilage from birth; in adults, after a long intubation or pressure from a tumour or goitre.
tracheomalacia.treatment: In children it usually goes away by age 2–3; severe cases need stents or surgery.

addison.name: Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease)
addison.desc: The adrenal cortex makes too little cortisol and aldosterone.
addison.symptoms: Weakness, weight loss, low blood pressure, craving salt, darkening of the skin.
addison.causes: Most often the immune system destroys the adrenal cortex; less often tuberculosis.
addison.treatment: Lifelong hormone tablets to replace the missing ones; the dose is raised during stress and illness.

cushing.name: Cushing's syndrome
cushing.desc: There is too much cortisol in the body.
cushing.symptoms: A round face, belly fat with thin arms and legs, purple stretch marks, high blood pressure, weak muscles, diabetes.
cushing.causes: Most often long-term use of steroid medicines; less often a tumour of the pituitary or an adrenal gland.
cushing.treatment: Gradually stopping the steroids if possible, or removing the tumour.

pheochromocytoma.name: Pheochromocytoma
pheochromocytoma.desc: A tumour of the adrenal medulla that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline into the blood.
pheochromocytoma.symptoms: Episodes of a sharp rise in blood pressure, pounding heartbeat, headache, sweating, pale skin.
pheochromocytoma.causes: Usually no clear cause; some cases are inherited.
pheochromocytoma.treatment: Removing the tumour after preparation with medicines that lower blood pressure.

conn.name: Primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome)
conn.desc: The adrenal glands make too much aldosterone.
conn.symptoms: Persistent high blood pressure that is hard to treat; low potassium causing weakness and cramps.
conn.causes: A small benign tumour of one adrenal gland or overgrowth of both adrenal glands.
conn.treatment: Removing the adrenal gland with the tumour, or medicines that block aldosterone.

appendix_tumors.name: Appendiceal tumors
appendix_tumors.desc: Rare tumours of the appendix; the most common is a neuroendocrine tumour, usually small and harmless.
appendix_tumors.symptoms: Usually none; they are often found by chance after the appendix is removed.
appendix_tumors.treatment: Removing the appendix, and for large tumours part of the large intestine.

mucocele.name: Appendiceal mucocele
mucocele.desc: The appendix becomes swollen with mucus trapped inside it.
mucocele.symptoms: Usually none; sometimes pain in the lower right abdomen, like appendicitis.
mucocele.causes: A blocked opening or a mucus-producing tumour.
mucocele.treatment: Careful removal: if the mucocele bursts, the mucus can spread through the abdominal cavity.

hemorrhoids.name: Hemorrhoids
hemorrhoids.desc: Clusters of blood vessels in the lower rectum swell, become inflamed and can prolapse.
hemorrhoids.symptoms: Bright red blood on the paper after a bowel movement, itching, lumps that come out, pain if a lump clots.
hemorrhoids.causes: Constipation and straining, long sitting, pregnancy, too little fibre.
hemorrhoids.treatment: Fibre and water, suppositories and creams; lumps can be banded with rubber rings or removed.

anal_fissure.name: Anal fissure
anal_fissure.desc: A small tear in the lining of the anus.
anal_fissure.symptoms: Sharp pain during and after a bowel movement, a little bright red blood.
anal_fissure.causes: Hard stools and constipation, less often diarrhoea.
anal_fissure.treatment: Soft stools thanks to fibre, warm baths, creams that relax the sphincter; surgery is rarely needed.

proctitis.name: Proctitis
proctitis.desc: Inflammation of the lining of the rectum.
proctitis.symptoms: Frequent false urges, mucus and blood in the stool, pain in the anus.
proctitis.causes: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, infections, radiotherapy to the pelvis.
proctitis.treatment: Treating the cause: anti-inflammatory suppositories and enemas, antibiotics for infections.

fibroids.name: Uterine fibroids
fibroids.desc: Benign tumours of the uterine muscle; very common, many women have them by age 50.
fibroids.symptoms: Often none; otherwise heavy, long periods, pelvic heaviness, frequent urges from pressure on the bladder.
fibroids.causes: They grow under the influence of estrogen; family history matters.
fibroids.treatment: Watching, hormone medicines, removing the fibroids or blocking the arteries that feed them. After menopause they usually shrink.

endometriosis.name: Endometriosis
endometriosis.desc: Tissue similar to the endometrium grows outside the uterus: on the ovaries, the lining of the abdomen, the bowel.
endometriosis.symptoms: Very painful periods, pelvic pain, difficulty getting pregnant.
endometriosis.causes: The exact cause is unknown; one theory is menstrual blood flowing back through the fallopian tubes.
endometriosis.treatment: Painkillers, hormone medicines, removing the patches during laparoscopy.

cervical_cancer.name: Cervical cancer
cervical_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the cervix; it is almost always caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV).
cervical_cancer.symptoms: No signs early on; later, bleeding after sex or between periods.
cervical_cancer.causes: Long-term infection with high-risk HPV types, smoking.
cervical_cancer.treatment: The HPV vaccine and regular smear tests prevent most cases. Treatment: surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

endometritis.name: Endometritis
endometritis.desc: Inflammation of the inner lining of the uterus, the endometrium.
endometritis.symptoms: Lower abdominal pain, fever, unusual discharge.
endometritis.causes: Infection after childbirth, abortion or procedures inside the uterus, sexually transmitted infections.

pcos.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
pcos.desc: A hormonal disorder: the ovaries have many immature follicles and ovulation is rare.
pcos.symptoms: Irregular or infrequent periods, acne, excess hair growth, weight gain, difficulty getting pregnant.
pcos.causes: Excess male hormones and insulin resistance; family history.
pcos.treatment: Weight loss, hormone medicines, drugs for insulin resistance, ovulation induction.

ovarian_cyst.name: Ovarian cyst
ovarian_cyst.desc: A fluid-filled sac in an ovary; most often a functional cyst from a follicle or the corpus luteum.
ovarian_cyst.symptoms: Usually none; a large cyst causes heaviness and pelvic pain.
ovarian_cyst.causes: A follicle did not burst at ovulation or the corpus luteum filled with fluid; less often endometriosis or tumours.
ovarian_cyst.treatment: Functional cysts go away on their own within 1–3 cycles; persistent and large ones are removed.

ovarian_cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the ovary; it is often found late.
ovarian_cancer.symptoms: Vague signs: bloating and a growing belly, feeling full quickly, pelvic pain.
ovarian_cancer.causes: Age, family history (BRCA gene mutations), endometriosis.
ovarian_cancer.treatment: Surgery and chemotherapy; carriers of BRCA mutations sometimes have the ovaries and tubes removed as a precaution.

ovarian_apoplexy.name: Ovarian apoplexy
ovarian_apoplexy.desc: A sudden rupture of an ovary with bleeding, usually at ovulation or from the corpus luteum.
ovarian_apoplexy.symptoms: Sharp pain on one side of the lower abdomen, weakness, dizziness with heavy bleeding.
ovarian_apoplexy.causes: A burst vessel in a follicle or the corpus luteum, sometimes after exercise or sex.
ovarian_apoplexy.treatment: Observation for light bleeding; surgery that saves the ovary for heavy bleeding.

prostatitis.name: Prostatitis
prostatitis.desc: Inflammation of the prostate, either an acute bacterial infection or a long-lasting condition.
prostatitis.symptoms: Pain between the legs and in the lower abdomen, frequent painful urination, fever in acute cases.
prostatitis.causes: Bacteria; in the chronic form the cause is often unclear.
prostatitis.treatment: Antibiotics for bacterial prostatitis; painkillers, relaxing medicines and physiotherapy for the chronic form.

bph.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
bph.desc: With age the prostate grows and squeezes the urethra.
bph.symptoms: A weak, stop-start stream, frequent urges, especially at night, a feeling that the bladder is not empty.
bph.causes: Age and male hormones: most men over 60 have it.
bph.treatment: Medicines that relax the bladder neck or shrink the gland; surgery if the squeezing is severe.

prostate_cancer.name: Prostate cancer
prostate_cancer.desc: A malignant tumour of the prostate; it often grows very slowly.
prostate_cancer.symptoms: No signs in the early stages; later, difficulty urinating and bone pain.
prostate_cancer.treatment: A PSA blood test and MRI help find it early. Slow tumours are watched, others are treated with surgery, radiotherapy or hormones.

aortic_aneurysm.name: Aortic aneurysm
aortic_aneurysm.desc: The aortic wall weakens and bulges out like a balloon. A large aneurysm can burst, causing life-threatening bleeding.
aortic_aneurysm.symptoms: Often none; it is found on an ultrasound. Sometimes a pulsing lump in the abdomen or pain in the belly or back.
aortic_aneurysm.causes: Atherosclerosis, high blood pressure, smoking, older age, inherited connective-tissue disorders.
aortic_aneurysm.treatment: A small one is watched with ultrasound and blood pressure is treated; a large one is replaced with a graft, by surgery or a stent-graft put in through an artery.

aortic_dissection.name: Aortic dissection
aortic_dissection.desc: Blood forces its way through a tear in the inner layer of the aorta and splits its wall apart. A medical emergency.
aortic_dissection.symptoms: Sudden tearing pain in the chest or back that may move; weakness, fainting, different blood pressure in the two arms.
aortic_dissection.causes: High blood pressure, atherosclerosis, inherited connective-tissue disorders (Marfan syndrome), injury.
aortic_dissection.treatment: Emergency care: blood pressure and heart rate are lowered; if the ascending part is affected, urgent surgery.

atherosclerosis.name: Atherosclerosis
atherosclerosis.desc: Plaques of fat and cholesterol build up in artery walls: the channel narrows and blood flow weakens.
atherosclerosis.symptoms: Unnoticed for a long time. Later it depends on where the narrowing is: chest pain on exertion, leg pain when walking, signs of stroke.
atherosclerosis.causes: Smoking, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, diabetes, excess weight, inactivity, age.
atherosclerosis.treatment: Quitting smoking, exercise, less animal fat in the diet; medicines for cholesterol and blood pressure; a stent or bypass for severe narrowing.

coarctation.name: Coarctation of the aorta
coarctation.desc: A narrowing of the aorta present from birth, usually just after the arch: pressure is high above it and low below it.
coarctation.symptoms: High blood pressure in the arms and a weak pulse in the legs, headaches, cold feet; in babies, fast breathing and poor weight gain.
coarctation.causes: The vessel develops abnormally before birth; it often comes with other heart defects.
coarctation.treatment: The narrowing is widened with a balloon and stent or removed by surgery; blood pressure is then checked for life.

svc_syndrome.name: Superior vena cava syndrome
svc_syndrome.desc: The superior vena cava is squeezed or blocked, so blood from the head, neck and arms cannot drain properly to the heart.
svc_syndrome.symptoms: Swelling of the face, neck and arms, bulging veins on the neck and chest, shortness of breath, cough, headache, worse when lying down.
svc_syndrome.causes: Most often a tumor in the chest (lung cancer, lymphoma); less often a clot around a catheter or pacemaker lead.
svc_syndrome.treatment: The cause is treated (chemotherapy or radiotherapy for a tumor), clots are dissolved with medicines; the vein can be opened with a stent.

ivc_thrombosis.name: Inferior vena cava thrombosis
ivc_thrombosis.desc: A blood clot partly or fully blocks the inferior vena cava; it often spreads up from clots in the leg or pelvic veins.
ivc_thrombosis.symptoms: Swelling and heaviness in both legs, enlarged veins on the belly, lower back pain; a piece of clot can break off and reach the lungs.
ivc_thrombosis.causes: Long immobility, surgery, tumors, pregnancy, blood that clots too easily, a filter placed in the vein.
ivc_thrombosis.treatment: Medicines that stop blood from clotting (anticoagulants); sometimes the clot is dissolved or removed through a catheter.

spinal_injury.name: Spinal cord injury
spinal_injury.desc: Damage to the spinal cord when the spine is injured: signals below the injury stop getting through.
spinal_injury.symptoms: Weakness or paralysis and loss of feeling below the level of injury, problems with breathing (neck injuries), bowels and bladder.
spinal_injury.causes: Road accidents, falls from height, diving into shallow water, sports injuries, wounds.
spinal_injury.treatment: Keeping the spine still right after the injury, urgent surgery, then long rehabilitation. A person who may have a spinal injury should not be moved unless necessary.

herniated_disc.name: Herniated disc
herniated_disc.desc: The jelly-like core of a disc between vertebrae bulges out through a crack and presses on a nerve root.
herniated_disc.symptoms: Pain in the lower back or neck that spreads into a leg or arm, numbness, tingling, muscle weakness.
herniated_disc.causes: Wear of the discs with age, lifting heavy things while bending, excess weight, sitting a lot, injury.
herniated_disc.treatment: Usually gets better without surgery: painkillers, exercises, physiotherapy; surgery if a nerve is badly compressed.

multiple_sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple_sclerosis.desc: The immune system damages the coating of nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord, so signals pass less well.
multiple_sclerosis.symptoms: Episodes of blurred vision, numbness, weakness in the arms and legs, unsteadiness, severe tiredness; it may improve between episodes.
multiple_sclerosis.causes: An autoimmune disease; the risk rises with family history, low vitamin D, smoking and past Epstein–Barr virus infection.
multiple_sclerosis.treatment: There is no cure yet, but medicines reduce flare-ups and slow the disease; steroids for flare-ups, rehabilitation.

carpal_tunnel.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
carpal_tunnel.desc: The median nerve is squeezed in a narrow tunnel in the wrist.
carpal_tunnel.symptoms: Numbness and tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, especially at night; weakness of the hand.
carpal_tunnel.causes: Repetitive hand movements, pregnancy, diabetes, an underactive thyroid, rheumatoid arthritis, wrist injuries.
carpal_tunnel.treatment: A wrist splint at night, breaks from work, sometimes steroid injections; if that fails, surgery to free the nerve.

myasthenia.name: Myasthenia gravis
myasthenia.desc: The immune system makes antibodies that block nerves from passing commands to muscles. It is often linked to the thymus.
myasthenia.symptoms: Muscle weakness that gets worse in the evening and after effort: drooping eyelids, double vision, trouble chewing and swallowing.
myasthenia.causes: An autoimmune disease; many patients have an enlarged thymus or a thymus tumor (thymoma).
myasthenia.treatment: Medicines that boost signal transmission and drugs that calm the immune system; the thymus is often removed by surgery.

thymoma.name: Thymoma
thymoma.desc: A tumor of thymus cells that usually grows slowly.
thymoma.symptoms: Often none; it is found on a chest scan. Sometimes cough, pain behind the breastbone, shortness of breath or signs of myasthenia gravis.
thymoma.causes: The cause is unknown; it is most common at 40–60 years of age.
thymoma.treatment: Removal of the thymus together with the tumor, plus radiotherapy or chemotherapy if needed.

pituitary_adenoma.name: Pituitary adenoma
pituitary_adenoma.desc: A benign tumor of the pituitary. It may release extra hormones or press on nearby nerves.
pituitary_adenoma.symptoms: Depends on the hormone: menstrual changes and nipple discharge, signs of acromegaly or Cushing's; a large tumor causes headaches and loss of side vision.
pituitary_adenoma.treatment: Some tumors shrink with medicines; others are removed by surgery through the nose, sometimes followed by radiotherapy.

acromegaly.name: Acromegaly
acromegaly.desc: An adult has too much growth hormone: the hands, feet, nose, jaw and internal organs get bigger.
acromegaly.symptoms: Rings and shoes get tight, facial features coarsen, gaps appear between the teeth, sweating, joint pain; in childhood the excess causes gigantism.
acromegaly.causes: Almost always a pituitary adenoma that releases growth hormone.
acromegaly.treatment: Surgery to remove the adenoma, medicines that block growth hormone, sometimes radiotherapy.

hypopituitarism.name: Hypopituitarism
hypopituitarism.desc: The pituitary releases too little of one or more hormones, so the glands it controls work less.
hypopituitarism.symptoms: Weakness, tiredness, feeling cold, low sex drive, menstrual changes; poor growth in children.
hypopituitarism.causes: Pituitary tumors and surgery, head injury, radiotherapy, bleeding into the pituitary.
hypopituitarism.treatment: Lifelong replacement of the missing hormones: thyroid, adrenal and sex hormones, growth hormone.

diabetes_insipidus.name: Diabetes insipidus
diabetes_insipidus.desc: There is not enough of the hormone vasopressin (or the kidneys do not respond to it), so the kidneys cannot hold on to water.
diabetes_insipidus.symptoms: A lot of pale urine, up to 10–20 liters a day, strong thirst, waking at night to urinate.
diabetes_insipidus.causes: Tumors and injuries around the pituitary and hypothalamus, surgery; less often inherited causes or kidney disease.
diabetes_insipidus.treatment: A vasopressin substitute (desmopressin) as tablets or nasal spray, drinking to thirst.

diaphragmatic_hernia.name: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia
diaphragmatic_hernia.desc: A baby is born with a hole in the diaphragm, and abdominal organs move into the chest and keep the lungs from growing.
diaphragmatic_hernia.symptoms: Severe breathing trouble right after birth, bluish skin, a sunken belly.
diaphragmatic_hernia.causes: The diaphragm does not close completely while the baby develops; the exact cause is usually unknown.
diaphragmatic_hernia.treatment: Intensive breathing support after birth, then surgery to close the hole. It is often found on an ultrasound during pregnancy.

diaphragm_paralysis.name: Diaphragm paralysis
diaphragm_paralysis.desc: The diaphragm, or half of it, stops contracting because the phrenic nerve is damaged.
diaphragm_paralysis.symptoms: Shortness of breath on exertion and when lying flat, poor sleep; paralysis of one side sometimes causes no symptoms.
diaphragm_paralysis.causes: Heart and neck surgery, injuries, chest tumors, viral infections, nerve and muscle diseases.
diaphragm_paralysis.treatment: It often recovers on its own over months; breathing machines at night help, sometimes surgery or a nerve stimulator.

hiccups.name: Persistent hiccups
hiccups.desc: Hiccups are sudden involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, each followed by the vocal cords snapping shut. They usually stop within minutes; persistent hiccups last more than two days.
hiccups.symptoms: Repeated 'hic' sounds that get in the way of eating, talking and sleeping.
hiccups.causes: Ordinary hiccups: overeating, fizzy drinks, alcohol, excitement; persistent ones may come with reflux, nervous-system or kidney disease, or some medicines.
hiccups.treatment: Ordinary hiccups stop on their own or after holding your breath or sipping cold water; persistent ones are investigated and the cause treated, sometimes with medicines.

lymphadenitis.name: Lymphadenitis
lymphadenitis.desc: Inflammation of a lymph node, usually caused by an infection nearby.
lymphadenitis.symptoms: The node is swollen and tender, the skin over it may turn red; fever, weakness.
lymphadenitis.causes: Sore throat, bad teeth, cuts and boils on the skin, childhood infections, less often tuberculosis or cat-scratch disease.
lymphadenitis.treatment: The source of infection is treated, with antibiotics for bacterial inflammation; a node full of pus is drained by a surgeon.

lymphoma.name: Lymphoma
lymphoma.desc: A cancer of immune cells called lymphocytes. It grows in the lymph nodes, spleen and other organs.
lymphoma.symptoms: Painless swollen nodes in the neck, armpits or groin, night sweats, unexplained fever, weight loss, itchy skin.
lymphoma.causes: Usually unknown; the risk is higher with a weakened immune system and some viral infections.
lymphoma.treatment: Chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiotherapy; many lymphomas can be cured.

lymphedema.name: Lymphedema
lymphedema.desc: Lymph does not drain well and builds up in the tissues, usually in an arm or leg.
lymphedema.symptoms: Lasting swelling, heaviness and tight skin; over time the skin hardens.
lymphedema.causes: Removal or radiotherapy of lymph nodes during cancer treatment, infections, injuries, lymphatic vessels that did not develop properly.
lymphedema.treatment: Hard to cure completely: lymphatic drainage massage, compression garments, exercises and skin care help.
